title: The Nest of the Missel Thrush
paragraphs: Dickon stood for two or three minutes, looking all around him while Mary watched. Then he began to walk about quietly, even more lightly than Mary had the first time she found herself inside the four walls. His eyes seemed to be drinking in everything: the gray trees with gray creepers climbing over them and hanging from their branches, the tangle along the walls and through the grass, and the evergreen alcoves with their stone seats and tall flower urns.
“I never thought I’d see this place,” he said at last, in a whisper.
“Did you know about it?” Mary asked.
She had spoken out loud, and he signaled to her to be quiet.
“We have to talk low,” he said, “or someone will hear us and wonder what’s going on in here.”
“Oh! I forgot!” said Mary. She was frightened, and she pressed her hand quickly over her mouth. When she had calmed down, she asked again, “Did you know about the garden?”
Dickon nodded.
“Martha told me there was a garden no one ever went into,” he answered. “We used to wonder what it was like.”
He stopped and looked around at the lovely gray tangle, and his round eyes had a strange, happy look.

“Eh! Just think of the nests there’ll be here come springtime,” he said. “It’d be the safest nesting place in England. No one ever comes near, and there are tangles of trees and roses to build in. I wonder that all the birds on the moor don’t nest here.”
Mistress Mary put her hand on his arm again without even knowing she did it.
“Will there be roses?” she whispered. “Can you tell? I thought maybe they were all dead.”
“Eh! No! Not them, not all of them!” he answered. “Look here!”

He stepped over to the nearest tree. It was a very old one, with gray lichen all over its bark, yet it held up a curtain of tangled sprays and branches. He took a thick knife out of his pocket and opened one of its blades.

“There’s plenty of dead wood that ought to be cut out,” he said. “And there’s a lot of old wood, but it grew some new last year. This is a new bit,” and he touched a shoot that looked brownish green instead of hard, dry gray.
Mary touched it herself, eagerly and with great care.
“This one?” she said. “Is it really alive? Quite alive?”
Dickon curved his wide, smiling mouth.
“It’s as wick as you or me,” he said. Mary remembered that Martha had told her “wick” meant “alive” or “lively.”
“Oh, I’m so glad it’s wick!” she cried in her whisper. “I want every one of them to be wick. Let’s walk around the whole garden and count the wick ones.”

She was nearly breathless with eagerness, and Dickon was just as eager. They went from tree to tree and from bush to bush. Dickon held his knife in his hand and showed her things that she thought were wonderful.

“They’ve run wild,” he said, “but the strongest ones have done well on it. The most delicate ones have died out, but the others have grown and grown, and spread and spread, till they’re a marvel. See here!” He pulled down a thick gray branch that looked dry. “A person might think this was dead wood, but I don’t believe it is, not all the way down to the root. I’ll cut it low down and see.”
He knelt and cut through the lifeless-looking branch with his knife, not far above the ground.
“There!” he said triumphantly. “I told you so. There’s still green in that wood. Look at it.”
Mary was down on her knees before he even spoke, staring with all her might.

“When it looks a bit green and juicy like that, it’s wick,” he explained. “When the inside is dry and snaps easily, like this piece I’ve cut off, it’s finished. There’s a big root here that all this live wood grew out of. If the old wood is cut away, and the soil is dug around it and looked after, there’ll be—” He stopped and lifted his face to look up at the climbing, hanging sprays above him. “There’ll be a fountain of roses here this summer.”

They went from bush to bush and from tree to tree. He was very strong and clever with his knife. He knew how to cut away the dry, dead wood, and he could tell when a poor-looking bough or twig still had green life in it. After half an hour Mary thought she could tell too. When he cut through a lifeless-looking branch, she would cry out with joy, under her breath, whenever she spotted the faintest shade of moist green. The spade, the hoe, and the fork were very useful. He showed her how to use the fork while he dug around the roots with the spade, stirring the earth and letting the air in.
They were hard at work around one of the biggest standard roses when he noticed something that made him gasp in surprise.
“Why!” he cried, pointing to the grass a few feet away. “Who did that?”
It was one of Mary’s own little clearings around the pale green points.
“I did it,” said Mary.
“Why, I thought you didn’t know anything about gardening,” he exclaimed.

“I don’t,” she answered. “But they were tiny, and the grass around them was thick and strong, and they seemed to have no room to breathe. So I cleared a space for them. I don’t even know what they are.”
Dickon went and knelt beside them, with his wide smile.

“You were right,” he said. “A gardener couldn’t have told you better. They’ll grow now like Jack’s beanstalk. These are crocuses and snowdrops, and these here are narcissuses,” he said, turning to another patch, “and here’s daffydowndillys. Eh! They’ll be a sight to see.”
He ran from one clearing to the next.
“You’ve done a lot of work for such a little lass,” he said, looking her over.
“I’m getting fatter,” said Mary, “and I’m getting stronger. I used to be tired all the time. When I dig, I’m not tired at all. I like the smell of the earth when it’s turned up.”

“It’s wonderful good for you,” he said, nodding wisely. “There’s nothing as nice as the smell of good clean earth, except the smell of fresh growing things when the rain falls on them. Many a day I go out on the moor when it’s raining, and I lie under a bush and listen to the soft swish of the drops on the heather, and I just sniff and sniff. The end of my nose twitches like a rabbit’s, Mother says.”
“Don’t you ever catch cold?” Mary asked, gazing at him in wonder. She had never seen such a funny boy, or such a nice one.

“Not me,” he said, grinning. “I’ve never caught a cold since I was born. I wasn’t brought up soft enough. I’ve run about the moor in all weathers, same as the rabbits do. Mother says I’ve sniffed up too much fresh air in twelve years ever to get a sniffle. I’m as tough as a hawthorn walking stick.”
He kept working the whole time he talked, and Mary followed him, helping with her fork or the trowel.
“There’s a lot of work to do here!” he said once, looking around with delight.
“Will you come back and help me with it?” Mary begged. “I’m sure I can be useful, too. I can dig and pull weeds and do anything you tell me. Oh! Please come, Dickon!”
“I’ll come every day if you want me, rain or shine,” he answered firmly. “It’s the best fun I’ve ever had in my life, shut in here and waking up a garden.”
“If you’ll come,” said Mary, “if you’ll help me make it alive, I’ll—I don’t know what I’ll do,” she ended helplessly. What could anyone do for a boy like that?

“I’ll tell you what you’ll do,” said Dickon, with his happy grin. “You’ll get fat, and you’ll get as hungry as a young fox, and you’ll learn to talk to the robin the way I do. Eh! We’ll have a lot of fun.”
He began to walk about, looking up into the trees and at the walls and bushes with a thoughtful face.

“I wouldn’t want to make it look like a gardener’s garden, all clipped and neat and tidy, would you?” he said. “It’s nicer like this, with things running wild and swinging and catching hold of each other.”
“Let’s not make it tidy,” said Mary anxiously. “It wouldn’t feel like a secret garden if it was tidy.”
Dickon stood rubbing his rusty-red head, looking rather puzzled.
“It’s a secret garden, sure enough,” he said, “but it seems to me someone besides the robin must have been in it since it was shut up ten years ago.”
“But the door was locked and the key was buried,” said Mary. “No one could get in.”
“That’s true,” he answered. “It’s a strange place. It seems to me as if there’s been a bit of pruning done here and there, later than ten years ago.”
“But how could that have happened?” said Mary.
He was looking closely at a branch of a standard rose, and he shook his head.
“Aye! How could it?” he murmured. “With the door locked and the key buried.”

Mistress Mary always felt that no matter how many years she lived, she would never forget that first morning when her garden began to grow. Of course, it did seem to begin to grow for her that morning. When Dickon started to clear places to plant seeds, she remembered what Basil had sung at her when he wanted to tease her.
“Are there any flowers that look like bells?” she asked.
“Lilies of the valley do,” he answered, digging away with the trowel, “and there’s Canterbury bells, and campanulas.”
“Let’s plant some,” said Mary.

“There’s lilies of the valley here already. I saw them. They’ll have grown too close together and we’ll have to separate them, but there’s plenty. The other kinds take two years to bloom from seed, but I can bring you some bits of plants from our cottage garden. Why do you want them?”
Then Mary told him about Basil and his brothers and sisters in India, and how she had hated them, and how they had called her “Mistress Mary Quite Contrary.”
“They used to dance around me and sing at me. They sang—

‘Mistress Mary, quite contrary,
How does your garden grow?
With silver bells, and cockle shells,
And marigolds all in a row.’
I just remembered it, and it made me wonder if there really were flowers like silver bells.”
She frowned a little and gave her trowel a rather spiteful jab into the earth.
“I wasn’t as contrary as they were.”
But Dickon laughed.

“Eh!” he said. As he crumbled the rich black soil, she saw that he was breathing in its scent. “There doesn’t seem to be any need for anyone to be contrary when there are flowers and such, and so many friendly wild things running about making homes for themselves, or building nests and singing and whistling, does there?”
Mary was kneeling beside him, holding the seeds. She looked at him and stopped frowning.
“Dickon,” she said, “you’re every bit as nice as Martha said. I like you, and that makes five people I like. I never thought I could like five people.”
Dickon sat back on his heels, the way Martha did when she was polishing the grate. He looked funny and delightful, Mary thought, with his round blue eyes and red cheeks and happy, turned-up nose.
“Only five folk you like?” he said. “Who are the other four?”
“Your mother and Martha,” Mary counted them off on her fingers, “and the robin and Ben Weatherstaff.”
Dickon laughed so hard that he had to muffle the sound by putting his arm over his mouth.
“I know you think I’m a queer lad,” he said, “but I think you’re the queerest little lass I ever saw.”

Then Mary did something strange. She leaned toward him and asked him a question she had never dreamed of asking anyone. She tried to say it in Yorkshire, because that was his own language, and in India a native was always pleased when you knew how he spoke.
“Do you like me?” she said, in Yorkshire.
“Eh!” he answered heartily, “that I do. I like you wonderful well, and so does the robin, I do believe!”
“That’s two, then,” said Mary. “That’s two for me.”
After that they worked harder than ever, and with more joy. Mary was startled and sorry when the big clock in the courtyard struck the hour for her midday dinner.
“I’ll have to go,” she said sadly. “And you’ll have to go too, won’t you?”
Dickon grinned.
“My dinner’s easy to carry around with me,” he said. “Mother always lets me put a bit of something in my pocket.”

He picked his coat up off the grass and pulled from its pocket a lumpy little bundle knotted in a coarse blue and white handkerchief, which was quite clean. Inside were two thick pieces of bread with a slice of something laid between them.
“It’s most often nothing but bread,” he said, “but today I’ve got a fine slice of fat bacon with it.”
Mary thought it looked like a queer dinner, but he seemed ready to enjoy it.
“Run along and get your dinner,” he said. “I’ll be finished with mine first. I’ll get some more work done before I start back home.”
He sat down with his back against a tree.
“I’ll call the robin up,” he said, “and give him the rind of the bacon to peck at. They like a bit of fat wonderfully well.”

Mary could hardly stand to leave him. All at once she felt he might be a kind of wood fairy, who would vanish before she came back into the garden. He seemed too good to be true. She walked slowly halfway to the door in the wall, then stopped and turned back.
“Whatever happens, you—you would never tell?” she said.
His poppy-colored cheeks were puffed out with his first big bite of bread and bacon, but he managed to smile encouragingly.
“If you were a missel thrush and showed me where your nest was, do you think I’d tell anyone? Not me,” he said. “You’re as safe as a missel thrush.”
And she was quite sure she was.
